papers.title: Plasma proteomic markers of cognitive and brain aging in a multi-ethnic cohort
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.26368682 v1

summary.one_liner: A plasma proteomics study measuring 220 blood proteins in 250 older adults from three ethnic groups, linking protein levels to cognition, brain MRI measures, and cognitive decline, with partial replication in 1,381 ADNI participants.
summary.plain: Researchers checked about 220 proteins in blood samples from 250 older adults of Chinese, South Asian, and non-Hispanic White background, and compared them with thinking test scores and brain scans. Blood levels of proteins tied to brain disease, nerve-cell connections, oxidative stress, and inflammation were linked to poorer cognition, and some inflammatory proteins were linked to signs of small blood-vessel damage in the brain. Several findings were then checked in a separate, much larger US dataset, the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
summary.why: Most Alzheimer's and brain-aging biomarker research has been done in mostly White populations, so testing these blood markers in more ethnically diverse groups is a useful check on whether they hold up more broadly. The findings point to candidate blood markers for brain aging, but the text does not show that they can be used clinically, and the associations described are not proof of cause.
summary.background:
- Proteomics: measuring large numbers of proteins at once in a blood sample.
- Plasma: the liquid part of blood, used here as the sample.
- Tau (pTau): a protein that forms tangles in Alzheimer's disease; phosphorylated forms are used as disease markers, and BDpTau is a brain-derived form measured in blood.
- Entorhinal cortex: a memory-related brain region that thins in early Alzheimer's.
- Small vessel disease: damage to the tiny blood vessels deep in the brain, often seen on MRI.
- Cardiometabolic risk: conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and obesity.
- Replication: testing earlier findings in a separate group to see if they hold.
- ADNI: a large, long-running US study of people with and without Alzheimer's disease.

papers.abstract: Advances in ultrasensitive proteomics offer opportunities to characterize molecular pathways underlying brain aging. We measured 220 plasma proteins using NULISAseq Neuro220 in 250 Chinese, South Asian, and non-Hispanic White older adults (mean age=68.2 years, 70.4% female). Proteins implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (including brain-derived phosphorylated Tau, BDpTau), synaptic function, oxidative stress, and inflammation were associated with poorer cognition. Phosphorylated Tau205 was associated with reduced entorhinal thickness, whereas inflammatory proteins were associated with imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease. Several findings were replicated in 1,381 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, including associations of BDpTau species, NPTX2, BACE1, TREM1, CCL17, PRDX6, and IGF1R with cognitive decline and clinical progression. Cardiometabolic risk factors were associated with widespread proteomic alterations, many of which were also linked to poorer brain health. These results identify promising molecular markers of brain aging and extend proteomic research to ethnically diverse populations historically underrepresented in Alzheimer's disease research.

papers.title: Nigral volume as a marker for Lewy body copathology in Alzheimer's disease
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368759 v1

summary.one_liner: In 73 ADNI participants with clinical Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment, lower antemortem neuromelanin-MRI substantia nigra volume tracked with autopsy-confirmed Lewy body copathology and with greater nigral hypopigmentation at autopsy, in a single-cohort study.
summary.plain: Some people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease also have Lewy body deposits, abnormal protein clumps in the brain that are more typical of Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. This study asked whether a special brain scan, which measures the size of a small midbrain region called the substantia nigra, can help spot those cases while people are still alive. Among 73 people who had both scans and autopsies, those with Lewy body deposits had a smaller nigral volume, and adding this measure improved a simple prediction model.
summary.why: Lewy body copathology is linked to earlier symptoms and faster cognitive decline, so a non-invasive way to flag it before death could matter for diagnosis and trial selection. The authors themselves note this is one cohort, with several years between scan and autopsy, so the result needs replication before it is relied on.
summary.background:
- Alzheimer's disease (AD): the most common dementia, marked by amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
- Lewy bodies: clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein found in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies; they can co-occur with AD.
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI): noticeable memory or thinking problems that do not yet meet the threshold for dementia.
- Substantia nigra: a midbrain area that produces dopamine and loses cells in Parkinson's disease; its dark color comes from neuromelanin.
- Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI: a scan sequence that makes the pigmented substantia nigra visible, so its size can be measured.
- Autopsy confirmation: the diagnosis of Lewy body pathology was made after death, which is the reference standard here.
- ADNI: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a large public research cohort.

papers.abstract: Background: Lewy body (LB) copathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with earlier symptom onset and faster cognitive decline. Depigmentation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) volume is seen in both Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. We examined whether lower antemortem SNc volume was associated with autopsy confirmed LB pathology in patients with AD or mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods: Seventy-three participants with a clinical diagnosis of AD or MCI, neuromelanin-sensitive MRI, and subsequent neuropathologic assessment from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative were studied. At autopsy, 33 participants had LB pathology (LB+) and 40 had no LB pathology (LB-). We compared SNc volume between groups using analysis of covariance adjusted for age and sex. Within the LB+ group, we assessed the association between SNc volume and nigral hypopigmentation using Spearman correlation. In a secondary analysis, we tested whether adding SNc volume to a logistic regression mode containing age, sex, and executive function improved model fit for autopsy-defined LB status. Results: LB+ participants had greater nigral hypopigmentation at autopsy and lower antemortem SNc volume than LB- participants. The adjusted mean difference in SNc volume (LB+ minus LB-) was -66 mm3 (95% confidence interval -115.9 to -16.2, P=0.010). Within the LB+ group, lower SNc volume was associated with greater hypopigmentation (Spearman rho;=-0.373, P=0.032). Among 71 participants with complete model data, adding SNc volume improved model fit (likelihood ratio=8.67, P=0.003). The combined model had an in sample area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.770 (95% confidence interval: 0.661-0.879). Conclusion: The correspondence between lower antemortem SNc volume and greater hypopigmentation at autopsy supports the use of neuromelanin-sensitive MRI to characterize nigral involvement in AD or MCI with LB copathology. These findings are based on a single cohort, and the interval of several years between imaging and autopsy limits how closely the pigmentation ratings reflect nigral integrity at imaging.

papers.title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368132 v1

summary.background:
- Neurodegenerative disorders: diseases where brain cells or their connections gradually lose function, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
- Small vessel disease: damage to the tiny blood vessels deep in the brain, often seen on scans as white matter lesions.
- Case-control comparison: comparing people with a condition against similar people without it.
- Transdiagnostic: a pattern that cuts across diagnostic labels rather than belonging to one disease.
- MRI measures: brain volume, white matter microstructure (how well the wiring is organised), tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity (how regions activity is synchronised at rest).
- UK Biobank protocol: a standardised brain-imaging method from a large UK population study, so results can be compared across groups.
- Medial frontal pole and cingulum: a front-middle brain region and a fibre bundle running along the inner brain; the paper links these to symptoms.
summary.one_liner: A case-control and transdiagnostic MRI study of 251 people with Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, small vessel disease, or healthy age-matched controls, using the UK Biobank imaging protocol, linking disease-specific and shared brain changes to symptoms such as apathy, fatigue, depression and cognitive deficits.
summary.plain: Several brain diseases that develop with age, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and small vessel disease, share symptoms like memory problems, low mood and tiredness. This study scanned 251 people with these conditions and healthy older adults using one standard brain-scan protocol, and compared their brain features. The authors found that each disease has some distinct brain changes, but also many changes that overlap across diseases.
summary.why: Shared symptoms are common across these conditions, and the study suggests that a few brain connections may be linked to particular symptoms regardless of diagnosis. This could help explain symptom variation in older people, but the findings come from a modest sample and would need confirmation in larger, independent studies before they guide care.

papers.abstract: Background: Neurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. Methods: We collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. Results: We replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

papers.title: Geographic heterogeneity of gut microbiome biomarkers across neurological conditions: sub-national discordance in ten cohorts from eleven cities in six countries
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368539 v1

summary.background:
- The gut microbiome is the community of bacteria living in the intestine; 16S rRNA sequencing is a common, relatively inexpensive way to identify which bacterial groups (taxa) are present.
- A "biomarker" here means a set of bacterial features used to tell apart people with and without a condition.
- Machine-learning classifiers are models trained on one dataset and scored on held-out data; AUC (area under the curve) measures discrimination, where 0.5 is no better than chance and 1.0 is perfect.
- "Transfer" means training on one cohort and testing on a different one, the key test of whether a signature generalizes.
- A "cohort" is a group of study participants recruited in a particular way, and cohort-specific differences (diet, medication, lab protocol, local environment) can confound results.
- Feature rankings compare which bacterial taxa a model relies on most; the paper reports these rankings did not agree across cohorts.
summary.one_liner: Reanalysis of ten public 16S rRNA gene sequencing cohorts (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and autism; 1,185 samples from eleven cities in six countries) showing that gut microbiome classifiers trained in one cohort transfer poorly to another, even between recruitment sites within a single city pair.
summary.plain: Researchers have proposed that certain gut bacteria could serve as signs of brain conditions such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and autism. This paper asks whether those signs hold up in other groups of people, and it reprocessed public gut-bacteria datasets from many cities to test this. Models that worked reasonably well inside their own dataset became close to guesswork when applied to a different population, and the drop did not depend on how far apart the places were.
summary.why: It bears directly on whether gut microbiome tests could ever be used as diagnostic tools, and it suggests that signatures from a single study may not generalize even across nearby sites. The text does not show how this would translate into clinical practice, so the implications for diagnosis remain uncertain.

papers.abstract: Gut microbiota composition has been associated with multiple neurological conditions, and candidate biomarkers have been proposed on the basis of these associations. Their usefulness presupposes that taxa altered in one population are also altered in others, a condition that is rarely verified. This work quantifies the extent to which it holds, and the geographic scale at which it ceases to do so. Ten public 16S rRNA gene sequencing cohorts of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and autism spectrum disorder, collected in eleven cities across six countries, were reprocessed from raw data, comprising 1,185 samples with uniform processing within each condition. Models trained and evaluated within a single cohort reached a mean AUC of 0.751 in Alzheimer's disease, 0.741 in autism spectrum disorder and 0.673 in Parkinson's disease. When applied to a different population, these values fell to 0.569, 0.542 and 0.551 respectively. The decline was not associated with geographic distance: transfer between cities within the same country was equivalent to transfer between continents. No taxon appeared among the twenty most important features in all cohorts of a given condition, and no correlation between rankings reached significance. Classifiers trained to predict cohort of origin, disregarding clinical group, reached AUC values of 0.87 to 1.00 using control subjects, and equivalent values using affected subjects. In one cohort with two recruitment centers and a single protocol, controls from both cities were separable (AUC 0.947), models did not transfer between centers (0.562 and 0.515), and their rankings correlated 0.003. Geographic heterogeneity of discriminant taxa operates below the national scale, which constrains the generalization of microbiome signatures derived from individual cohorts.

papers.title: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368528 v1

summary.background:
- Epilepsy: a condition with recurring seizures; here the focus is on seizures arising in both temporal lobes (bitemporal).
- Responsive neurostimulation: a device that detects abnormal brain activity and delivers electrical pulses in response.
- Electrocorticography (ECoG): recording brain electrical activity with electrodes placed on the brain surface.
- Circadian rhythm: a roughly 24-hour biological cycle, such as sleep-wake timing.
- Hippocampus: a brain region involved in memory; the study compares its left and right sides.
- Kuramoto oscillator model: a mathematical model of many rhythmic units that synchronize with one another, used here to describe how the two hippocampi's rhythms align.
- In silico: carried out in computer simulation rather than in patients.
summary.one_liner: Longitudinal ECoG study in bitemporal epilepsy reporting that daily alignment of hippocampal connectivity rhythms predicts seizure reduction under responsive neurostimulation, modeled with a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator and in-silico stimulation-timing optimization.
summary.plain: This paper looks at whether the body's daily (roughly 24-hour) cycles affect how well brain stimulation works for epilepsy. The researchers followed people with seizures starting in both temporal lobes over months, recording brain activity from electrodes on the brain surface. They found that when the rhythms in the left and right hippocampus (a memory-related brain region) lined up in time, patients had more seizure reduction, and the timing of when stimulation was delivered during the day was linked to how these rhythms changed.
summary.why: It suggests that the timing of stimulation within the day, not just its amount, may matter for treatment, which could inform personalized neurostimulation for epilepsy and possibly other brain disorders. The text itself does not show that timing-based stimulation improves outcomes in patients; the timing optimization was only tested in simulation.

papers.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Carotid Artery Stenosis is Associated with Restless Legs Syndrome in the Absence of Stroke
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368361 v1

summary.background:
- Restless legs syndrome (RLS): a common disorder causing uncomfortable leg sensations and a strong urge to move, usually worse at rest or at night.
- Internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS): narrowing of the main arteries on each side of the neck that carry blood to the brain.
- Chronic hypoperfusion: long-term reduced blood flow to brain tissue.
- Dopaminergic pathways: brain circuits using dopamine, a chemical messenger; these are thought to be involved in RLS.
- Retrospective case-control study: looks back at existing records, comparing people with and without an exposure.
- Propensity score matching: pairing patients on many background traits so the groups are comparable.
- Odds ratio (OR): a measure of how much more likely an outcome is in one group; 1.09 means about 9% higher odds, a small effect.
- Confidence interval (CI): the range of values consistent with the data; this one is narrow and just above 1.
- Absolute risk difference: 1.977% vs 1.816%, about 0.16 percentage points.
summary.one_liner: A TriNetX propensity-matched case-control study (58,382 per group) reports a small association between bilateral internal carotid artery stenosis/occlusion (ICD-10 I65.23) and later restless legs syndrome diagnosis (G25.81), with an adjusted OR of 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186).
summary.plain: Restless legs syndrome is a common condition that causes an urge to move the legs, often at night. This study asked whether narrowing or blockage of the large arteries in the neck that supply the brain is linked to getting that condition, even when the person has not had a stroke. Using a large database of electronic health records, the researchers compared patients with severe bilateral neck-artery narrowing to similar patients with hardening of the arteries but no narrowing, and found a small increase in restless legs diagnoses.
summary.why: If a blood-flow problem in the brain contributes to restless legs, that would add a possible vascular cause to a condition usually treated as neurological or iron-related. The effect is small, though, and the study is observational, so it only suggests a link and cannot show that narrowed arteries cause the condition. The authors themselves call for prospective studies.

papers.abstract: Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson's disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression. Results: RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005-0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186), indicating a modest but significant association. Conclusion: Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.

papers.title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368410 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease: a progressive neurological disorder affecting movement, with growing non-motor symptoms including cognition.
- Deep brain stimulation (DBS): surgically implanted electrodes that send electrical pulses into a deep brain target; here the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
- Cognitive decline: worsening of thinking skills such as attention, memory and planning.
- Diffusion MRI: an MRI technique that measures how water molecules move in brain tissue, reflecting tissue structure.
- NODDI-DTI: two diffusion-MRI models; they estimate fibre organisation and tissue density/complexity in more detail than standard imaging.
- Brain networks: groups of regions that work together, here frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual.
- Voxel-wise analysis: comparing brain imaging values at every small 3D point across the brain.
- Open-label: patients and clinicians knew the treatment given; no control group blinding is implied.
summary.one_liner: A prospective open-label study of 40 Parkinson's patients using NODDI-DTI diffusion MRI finds that preoperative white-matter and grey-matter microstructure within three large-scale brain networks is associated with greater cognitive decline six months after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation.
summary.plain: Deep brain stimulation is an implanted electrode treatment that eases movement and other symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease, but about 15 to 20 percent of patients have thinking abilities worsen afterward. Researchers scanned 40 patients' brains with a special MRI method before surgery and again tested their thinking six months later. They found that poorer tissue quality in several brain networks before surgery was linked to bigger declines in cognition.
summary.why: If brain scans taken before surgery can flag who is at risk of thinking decline, clinicians could counsel patients more individually and monitor them more closely. The text suggests the findings point to both existing disease damage and the stimulation itself as contributors, but the study's size and open-label design mean the predictive value still needs confirmation in other groups.

papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

papers.title: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and clinical progression in early sporadic Parkinson's disease
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368420 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease: a progressive brain disorder affecting movement, with cognitive and balance problems over time.
- Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA): a lab test on spinal fluid that detects misfolded alpha-synuclein protein, used here to confirm the disease biology.
- Sporadic: not caused by a known inherited gene change.
- Plasma biomarkers: molecules measured in a blood sample that reflect activity or damage in tissues such as the brain.
- P-tau217: a form of tau protein linked to brain changes, often studied in Alzheimer's disease.
- NfL (neurofilament light chain): a protein released when nerve fibres are damaged.
- GFAP: a protein from support cells (astrocytes) in the brain, rising with injury or inflammation.
- Amyloid-beta (Aβ40, Aβ42): proteins that can accumulate in the brain; measured only in the Parkinson's group.
- PPMI (Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative): a large longitudinal study that collects detailed clinical and biological data.
- Tertiles: dividing participants into three equal-sized groups by biomarker level.
- Hazard: the instantaneous risk of an event occurring over time, used in time-to-event models.
summary.one_liner: In early sporadic Parkinson's disease with confirmed alpha-synuclein seeding in CSF, baseline plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels were associated with later cognitive and balance decline in PPMI participants compared with healthy controls.
summary.plain: This study looks at simple blood tests that measure signs of nerve-cell damage in people with early Parkinson's disease, compared with healthy people. Researchers measured several proteins in blood samples taken at the start of the study and then tracked participants' thinking and balance for up to 11 years. They found that higher levels of three of these markers were linked to worse later outcomes in the Parkinson's group, though the blood levels themselves did not differ between the two groups.
summary.why: If blood markers can flag which early patients are likely to decline, they could help design clinical trials and guide care, but the text is an association study and does not show that the markers cause or can reliably predict decline for individuals. Its relevance to treatment decisions remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.

papers.title: Imaging and Motor Asymmetry in Parkinson's Disease associated with GBA and LRRK2 mutations: Data from the PPMI study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368329 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease (PD) involves loss of dopamine-producing nerve cells, which is seen on DaT scans (a radioactive tracer that binds dopamine transporters in the striatum: caudate and putamen).
- Alpha-synuclein is a protein that clumps abnormally in PD; the SOC model proposes two subtypes: a symmetric "body-first" form with widespread spread and early non-motor symptoms, and an asymmetric "brain-first" form with early, localized motor symptoms.
- GBA and LRRK2 are genes; variants in them raise the risk of PD.
- iRBD (idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder) is a sleep condition where people act out dreams and often later develop a synucleinopathy.
- PPMI is a large public research database of Parkinson's patients and controls.
- MDS-UPDRS III is a standard clinical rating scale for motor symptoms.
- Asymmetry index and absolute asymmetry difference are ways of quantifying left-right imbalance.
summary.one_liner: Cross-sectional PPMI analysis comparing the left-right symmetry of dopamine-transporter imaging and MDS-UPDRS III motor scores in GBA-PD, LRRK2-PD, idiopathic PD and iRBD, used to test whether the SOC subtype model applies to genetic PD.
summary.plain: Parkinson's disease often starts on one side of the body and can differ in how it spreads through the brain. This study looked at people with Parkinson's caused by two known gene changes (GBA and LRRK2), compared them with people with no known genetic cause, and with people at risk who have a sleep disorder that often precedes Parkinson's. The researchers measured how evenly brain scan signals and motor symptoms were split between the left and right sides.
summary.why: It tests whether a proposed model that sorts Parkinson's into two subtypes also holds for genetic forms, which matters for how patients might be grouped in future studies and trials. The text reports that GBA-PD looked more symmetric and LRRK2-PD did not fit the model, and suggests a possible reason, but this is an observational association and the authors' explanation is speculative.

papers.abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.

papers.title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368344 v1

summary.background:
- Alzheimer's disease (AD): a progressive brain disease that causes memory and thinking decline; amyloid protein buildup is an early hallmark.
- Preclinical AD: amyloid or other brain changes are present but symptoms are not yet obvious.
- White matter: the brain's wiring (nerve fibers), which is wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating layer.
- Demyelination: loss of myelin insulation, which slows nerve signals.
- Axonal damage: injury to the nerve fiber itself.
- Wallerian degeneration: nerve fibers degenerating after their connected cell bodies are damaged, so damage spreads along the wiring.
- Gray matter: the outer layers of brain tissue where nerve cell bodies sit.
- APOE genotype: a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's risk.
- Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR): a standard scale for staging dementia severity.
- AUC (area under the curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a model separates groups; 0.933 is high.
summary.one_liner: A study introducing Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI), an MRI method sensitive to white matter microstructure, which separates two white matter phenotypes (axonal versus myelin changes) with different trajectories across the Alzheimer's disease continuum in 305 adults.
summary.plain: Alzheimer's disease damages the brain's wiring as well as its gray matter, but the wiring damage is hard to measure in living people. This paper describes an MRI-based technique that splits white matter changes into two types: damage to the nerve fibers themselves, and loss of their myelin insulation. The researchers tracked these in 305 adults ranging from people without amyloid to those with early symptoms.
summary.why: The text reports that the two phenotypes relate differently to later cognitive decline, with the axonal type showing the strongest link (41% of explained variance), and that the RKI metrics added to a model classifying clinical impairment. This may help with earlier tracking of disease, but the text does not show clinical use, and the findings come from a single cohort reported in the abstract only.

papers.abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

papers.title: α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity is associated with motor progression in the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368235 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease (PD) is a brain disorder involving loss of movement control; the "prodromal" stage is the period of early signs before a diagnosis is made.
- Alpha-synuclein is a brain protein that can misfold and clump; these clumps are thought to drive PD and related conditions.
- A seed amplification assay (SAA) copies tiny amounts of misfolded protein in a lab so they can be detected; "kinetic parameters" describe how fast the reaction proceeds.
- MDS-UPDRS Part III is a standard clinical motor exam score; Hoehn and Yahr is a 5-step disease stage scale; MoCA is a cognitive screening test.
- Phenoconversion means progressing from the prodromal state to a full diagnosis (here PD or dementia with Lewy bodies).
- Linear mixed-effects models track changes over time in repeated measurements; time-to-event analysis estimates the risk of an event over time, with hazard ratios comparing groups.
summary.one_liner: In the PPMI prodromal cohort, baseline alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) positivity was associated with faster MDS-UPDRS Part III motor progression over up to 12 years, persisting after excluding phenoconverters, and with higher hazard of phenoconversion to Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, while assay kinetic parameters were not associated with phenoconversion.
summary.plain: This study looks at people who show early warning signs of Parkinson's disease but do not yet have a full diagnosis. A lab test that detects a misfolded protein clump (alpha-synuclein) was run at the start, and researchers tracked these people's movement scores, stage ratings and thinking scores for up to 12 years. Those who tested positive got worse on movement scores faster than those who tested negative, and they were much more likely to develop the disease later.
summary.why: If a blood or spinal-fluid test can flag who is likely to decline, it could help choose participants for future trials of treatments that aim to slow the disease. The authors suggest this as a prognostic marker, but the work is observational, so it shows association rather than proof that the test should guide care.

papers.abstract: Background-Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinsons disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. MethodsClinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinsons Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. ResultsWe identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. ConclusionsBaseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.

papers.title: Modifiable and Context-Specific Factors Associated with Dementia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Community-Derived Cross-Sectional Study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368211 v1

summary.background:
- Dementia: a group of conditions causing progressive loss of memory and thinking skills.
- Cross-sectional study: data collected at one point in time; it can show that factors and conditions occur together but not which came first.
- Logistic regression: a statistical method that estimates how the odds of an outcome change with each factor; an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) above 1 means higher odds, below 1 means lower odds.
- Nagelkerke pseudo R-squared: a rough 0 to 1 measure of how much a model explains outcome differences, not the same as R-squared in ordinary regression.
- Bootstrap: a resampling method that re-runs the analysis many times to estimate uncertainty.
- Mean imputation: filling in missing values with the average; obesity data were 79.9% missing, so that result is weak.
- PM2.5: fine airborne particles from pollution.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional study of 721 community participants in the Democratic Republic of the Congo tests how 16 social, behavioral, and environmental factors relate to dementia status, and how much they add to a model that already includes age and sex.
summary.plain: This paper looks at what might be linked to dementia, a condition that affects memory and thinking, in people living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The researchers compared 232 people without cognitive impairment with 489 people who had dementia, and checked 16 factors such as poverty, education, mood, and alcohol use. Poverty, low resilience, and depression were linked to higher odds of dementia, while more education was linked to lower odds.
summary.why: Evidence on dementia from Central Africa is scarce, so a study from this region adds data that most dementia research has not covered. The authors note the sample is not representative and that the data cannot show cause and effect, so the findings are best read as associations that may point to areas for further study.

papers.abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

papers.title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.26368080 v1

summary.background:
- Epilepsy: recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Functional seizures look similar but come from a different cause, not abnormal electrical discharges, so telling them apart matters.
- Focal vs generalized epilepsy: seizures starting in one area of the brain versus seizures involving both sides from the outset.
- Drug-resistant epilepsy: seizures that continue despite trials of appropriate medicines.
- T1-weighted MRI: a standard brain scan that measures brain structure, such as cortical thickness and the volume of deep brain structures.
- Diffusion MRI: a scan that tracks how water moves along white-matter fibres; fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity are summary measures of this.
- Normative modeling: comparing one person's measurements with a large reference group of healthy people, expressed as how many standard deviations away they fall.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0.5 score means chance and 1.0 means perfect separation. Values around 0.6 are weak.
- Multiple-comparison correction (Benjamini-Hochberg): an adjustment that reduces false positives when many tests are run.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective study of 273 patients with epilepsy and 32 with functional seizures tests whether normative brain-deviation scores from clinical T1 and diffusion MRI can separate epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, and drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy, finding little discrimination in the primary analyses.
summary.plain: Doctors sometimes must tell apart different kinds of seizure disorders from brain scans, but the scans often look normal or show abnormalities spread across the brain. This study asked whether comparing each patient's scan with a large group of healthy people could help sort patients into these groups. In the main analyses it did not: none of the regional or tract measures separated the groups well, and the best overall signal, a general measure of how far the whole brain deviated from healthy norms, only modestly separated epilepsy from functional seizures.
summary.why: The paper is a useful check on a promising idea: normative brain-comparison methods were proposed as a route to individual-level biomarkers in epilepsy, and this work reports that such measures, as applied to routine clinical scans, do not yet support individual classification. It may matter for how much weight future imaging tools are given in epilepsy care, though the authors' suggested next steps (network-level analysis and combining data types) are proposals, not tested results.

papers.abstract: Background and ObjectivesNormative modeling expresses an individuals brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. MethodsWe retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). ResultsWe included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. DiscussionUnivariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

papers.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.26368127 v1

summary.background:
- Vergence: the inward (convergence) or outward (divergence) turning of the eyes so both point at the same object at different distances.
- Saccade: a fast, jerky eye movement that shifts gaze from one point to another.
- Gaze holding: keeping the eyes steady on a target once they are aligned.
- Subthalamic nucleus (STN): a small brain region involved in starting and stopping movements; deep brain stimulation (DBS) delivers electrical pulses through an implanted electrode.
- Parkinson's disease: a movement disorder caused by loss of certain brain cells that control movement.
- White-matter pathways: bundles of nerve fibers connecting brain regions. The field of Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways are two such bundles discussed here.
- Modeled stimulation anatomy: estimates, from computer models, of which fiber bundles the electrical current reaches around each electrode.
- Go/no-go control: the brain's process of deciding whether to start or hold back an action.
summary.one_liner: In 23 people with Parkinson's disease, switching subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation on and off changed how the eyes converge and how steadily they hold alignment, with effects linked to modeled stimulation location in white-matter pathways.
summary.plain: People with Parkinson's disease often have implanted electrodes that stimulate a deep brain region, and this study asked how that stimulation affects the coordinated movement of both eyes. Researchers recorded eye movements with the stimulator on and off, then compared the results with computer models of where the current spread in the brain. Stimulation reduced how much the eyes wobbled after they had moved into alignment, and the size of this change was linked to stimulation reaching particular nerve-fiber bundles.
summary.why: Keeping both eyes aligned is a simple, measurable window into how the basal ganglia and cerebellum shape movement, which may help guide more targeted stimulation in Parkinson's. The links to specific pathways are based on modeling and correlations in a modest sample, so they are suggestive rather than settled.

papers.abstract: ObjectiveClear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. MethodsWe used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinsons disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. ResultsCombined saccade-vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade-assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7-49.3%; p{approx}0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. ConclusionsThese findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. SignificanceBinocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

papers.title: Privilege Is Not Enough: Evaluating Generalized Distillation for Normative Brain Age Modeling in Depression, Anxiety and Alcohol Use Disorder
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368025 v1

summary.background:
- Generalized distillation: training a simple "student" model to imitate a stronger "teacher" that was trained on extra information (privileged data) the student will not have at use time.
- Brain-age gap: estimated brain age minus actual age; larger positive gaps are often read as signs of accelerated brain aging, though interpretation is debated.
- Normative modeling: building a reference of typical values (here, typical brain age for a given age) and measuring how far an individual deviates.
- Structural MRI (brain anatomy) and functional MRI (brain activity patterns) are the imaging inputs; biosocial data means non-imaging factors such as health and lifestyle measures.
- UK Biobank: a large UK research database of volunteers with health, imaging and lifestyle data.
- Gap-severity association: how strongly brain-age gaps track symptom severity or disorder severity.
summary.one_liner: Evaluates whether generalized distillation, where a student model trained on deployable features learns from a teacher trained on richer privileged data, yields brain-age gaps that match the teacher's clinically meaningful associations in depression, anxiety and alcohol use disorder using UK Biobank data.
summary.plain: Some medical prediction tools are trained on detailed scans and test results that are not available in everyday clinics. This paper asks whether a simpler model, using only what a clinic can actually collect, can learn from a model trained on the richer data and still reflect the same clinically useful patterns. It reports simulations and UK Biobank analyses in which these simpler "student" models usually produced brain-age gaps closer to their "teacher" models than comparable baselines did.
summary.why: Brain-age gaps, the difference between a scan-based age estimate and a person's real age, are studied as a marker of brain health in psychiatry, so a way to get such markers from cheaper inputs could matter in practice. The text reports success in 10 of 12 comparisons and notes that gains were largest where the teacher most beat the baseline, but it does not show that these markers improve diagnosis or treatment, so its clinical value remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Models trained on rich multimodal data may depend on modalities unavailable at deployment. In generalized distillation, a teacher trained on such privileged data guides a student using only deployable features. We ask whether students inherit clinically meaningful properties beyond predictions in brain-age modeling, where brain-age gaps index deviations from normative aging and brain health. In simulations, distillation recovered a gap-severity association which an age-trained baseline missed. In UK Biobank analyses of depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder, students using structural MRI, functional MRI or biosocial data produced gaps closer to their teachers than matched baselines in 10 of 12 comparisons. Where teachers most exceeded baselines (anxiety in biosocial, alcohol use in functional MRI students), gap-severity associations rose toward their teachers. Our findings characterize conditions for successful distillation, i.e. clinical signal the teacher holds, the baseline misses and deployable features contain, and demonstrate their relevance in a real-life psychiatry application.

papers.title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367865 v1

summary.background:
- Alzheimer's disease: a brain disease causing progressive memory loss; "early-onset" means starting before about age 65.
- PSEN1: a gene that makes presenilin-1, a protein involved in cutting other proteins in brain cells; variants in it are the most common known cause of early-onset familial Alzheimer's.
- Loss-of-function vs gain-of-function: a loss-of-function variant reduces or removes a gene's activity; a gain-of-function variant makes the protein act abnormally or more strongly.
- Stop-gain (nonsense) variant: a DNA change that inserts an early "stop" signal, producing a truncated protein.
- Nonsense-mediated decay: a cell quality-control process that destroys messages carrying early stop signals, so little protein is made.
- Splicing: the process that cuts out non-coding parts of a gene's message and joins the rest; a faulty splice site can remove pieces of the protein.
- In-frame deletion: removal of a whole number of amino acid building blocks, keeping the rest of the reading frame intact.
summary.one_liner: Genetic carriers of predicted loss-of-function PSEN1 variants (nonsense-mediated decay) showed no early-onset dementia, and re-analysis of the p.K109* variant suggests it instead disrupts splicing to create an in-frame deletion.
summary.plain: Some inherited mutations in a gene called PSEN1 strongly raise the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease before age 65, but scientists have debated whether they work by breaking the gene's protein or by making it do something harmful. The authors looked at 45 people across three large databases who carry mutations that should switch the gene off entirely, and found none had early-onset dementia. They also found that a previously reported mutation likely changes how the gene's message is cut and pieced together, rather than simply stopping it.
summary.why: The result bears on whether drugs that reduce PSEN1 activity could be safe, since it suggests that fully switching off the gene does not cause early-onset Alzheimer's. It is a focused genetic study, so its conclusions depend on how accurately the databases record diagnoses and on the small number of carriers.

papers.abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimers disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimers Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded diagnosis of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.
